title: How AI Threatens Capitalism
author: John B. Judis
content:
![How AI Threatens
Capitalism](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-19-at-7.21.21
---AM.png)

A recent Reddit
[_post_](https://www.reddit.com/r/Futurology/comments/1q43g77/so_ai_takes_over_everyone_has_lost_their_job_and/?ref=compactmag.com)
asks: "So, AI takes over, everyone has lost their job and only 10
trillionaires own everything. Now what?" The author goes on: "Meta, Open AI,
and Amazon own everything, cool beans! No one can work; therefore, no one has
money to buy any of the horse shit temu slop they prime on Amazon now. Won't
everything just implode from there?" The post gives voice to the anxiety and
despair that has greeted recent advances in artificial intelligence. Many
foresee a future in which America becomes a hellscape of unemployment and
penury, in which data centers and ghost towns prevail outside of the fortified
coastal retreats where tech oligarchs live.

Does it have to be that way? Sixty years ago, a discussion of computer
automation took place that was the opposite in tone and tenor. In 1964,
Michael Harrington, Robert Theobald, Robert Heilbroner, and a host of other
leading progressive figures of the era issued a memorandum entitled "The
Triple Revolution," in which they
[_predicted_](https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/newspape/isr/vol25/no03/adhoc.html?ref=compactmag.com)
that the "cybernetic revolution" would result in "potentially unlimited output
... that will require little cooperation from human beings." Such utopian
speculations were common at the time. Marshall McLuhan, in _Understanding
Media_ , predicted automation would encourage "imaginative participation in
society."

Needless to say, these dreams of post-industrial abundance didn't come to
pass. But a less well-remembered document of the same period, while affected
by the same blithe optimism, laid out a framework for understanding
technological change that could help us understand the challenges we face
today. In 1969, a small circulation journal, _Radical America_ , published a
[_long
essay_](https://files.libcom.org/files/Rad%20America%20V3%20I3.pdf?ref=compactmag.com)
by the historian Martin J. Sklar entitled, "On the Proletarian Revolution and
the End of Political Economy." Basing his analysis on a neo-Marxist framework
that may be relevant today, particularly with the emergence of artificial
intelligence, Sklar offered a theory of what he called the "disaccumulation of
capital" that provides a window through which to view the liberatory promise,
as well as the looming peril, of automation. It is a difficult read--Sklar
said it was written for "militant readers"--but it helps explain what is
happening to the American economy today.

Sklar took his cue from Karl Marx's theory of capital accumulation. For Marx,
the central engine of growth is the accumulation of capital, which he regards
as equivalent to the accumulation of labor time. According to the labor theory
of value--which was embraced by Adam Smith and David Ricardo as well as Marx--
the exchange value of consumer goods and of capital goods (plant, equipment,
raw materials) is measured in the labor time it takes to produce them. There
have been numerous byzantine attempts to create a formula that would convert
exchange values into prices, but the usefulness of Marx's theory doesn't rest
on that. The labor theory is a way of describing the labor process and
division of labor that takes place in capitalist production.

The accumulation of capital, achieved when the profit from sales is invested,
consists of the accumulation of labor time. Thus, during the period of rapid
industrialization from the Civil War to the 1920s, there was not just an
accumulation of goods and factories, but also of work-hours and of workers.
From 1900 to 1920, for instance, the number of manufacturing workers doubled
from five to ten million. As Marx stated in
[__Capital__](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/download/pdf/Capital-
Volume-I.pdf?ref=compactmag.com), "Accumulation of capital is, therefore,
increase of the proletariat." America looked at the time as if it were going
to become a giant factory with a labor force divided between a sprawling
working class and small capitalist class. This vision of the future informed
the socialism of Eugene Debs as well as the progressivism of Herbert Croly and
Thorstein Veblen. This accumulation of capital entailed a Protestant ethic of
deferred consumption. The business class cited the deferral of consumption for
investment and saving as the justification for its existence and also as the
justification for reducing wages or resisting demands to increase wages or to
limit the work week. Work, thrift, saving, and efficiency were the moral and
economic guideposts to capital accumulation.

But according to Sklar--and he had copious data to prove it--during the 1920s,
the output of goods soared but the hours spent producing them, and the number
of workers engaged in producing them, stopped increasing. What he called the
"disaccumulation of capital" began. He didn't think disaccumulation would
immediately replace accumulation, but that it was becoming a persistent
tendency within capitalism. It would replace accumulation only under
socialism.
